analysis.one_liner: Requires double hulls and spill-response plans for oil tankers in Puget Sound.
analysis.headline: The Puget Sound tanker safety bill was introduced after the Exxon Valdez spill but never got a hearing or a vote — it died in the Senate Commerce Committee with only two actions on the record.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Exxon Valdez spill in Alaska, this bill would have required new large oil tankers serving U.S. waters to have double hulls, forced tankers and oil facilities in Puget Sound to file detailed spill-prevention and cleanup plans, and required annual inspections and practice drills. It also directed the Coast Guard's department to push for tougher international tanker standards. The bill never left committee, so none of this took effect through this bill.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, and fish around Puget Sound would gain a margin of protection against catastrophic oil spills: double hulls reduce the oil released in a grounding or collision [S3], individualized spill plans, equipment requirements, annual inspections, and publicized practice drills aim to make responses faster and more honest about what equipment actually exists [S3]. Washington State would keep, and could share in, authority over spill planning, since the bill explicitly preserves state power and allows delegation of plan approval to the state [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Puget Sound communities, fisheries, and coastal economies

how_it_helps.text: Requires new tankers of 20,000 gross tons or more to have double sides and a double bottom throughout their cargo length — the design feature whose absence made the Exxon Valdez spill so large — for tankers operating in U.S. waters or transferring oil in U.S. ports.

Requires every tank vessel carrying oil in Puget Sound to prepare an individualized spill prevention plan covering notification procedures, assigned personnel, response equipment, and crew training, with a Coast Guard-issued equipment list and annual inspections to confirm compliance.

Requires vessel owners and oil-producing, refining, and transportation facilities near Puget Sound to submit government-approved contingency plans built around a published 'maximum probable spill' estimate, and lets the Secretary delegate plan approval to Washington State.

Mandates that the government annually publish the contingency plans and an equipment inventory, and run practice drills with a public report on actual response times — so residents can see whether spill response is real or on paper.

Backs the rules with civil penalties of up to $25,000 per day for continuing violations, ship-based liability, and criminal fines up to $50,000 and five years' imprisonment for willful violations, while preserving state authority to regulate oil vessels in state waters.

analysis.who_pays: Oil tanker owners and operators, and oil-producing, refining, and transportation facilities around Puget Sound, would bear the costs: fitting new double-hulled tankers, preparing and maintaining approved contingency plans, buying and stowing required response equipment, and passing annual inspections [S2, S3]. Violations could bring civil penalties of up to $25,000 per day and criminal penalties up to $50,000 and five years in prison [S3]. Some of these compliance costs would ultimately be reflected in the price of moving and refining oil.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil tanker owners and petroleum facilities

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls on the oil shipping and refining industry — new double-hulled tankers are substantially more expensive to build, and every covered vessel and facility would need approved contingency plans, equipment, and annual inspections — costs that would partly flow into oil transport prices.

A double hull mandate applies only to new tankers, so existing single-hulled ships could keep calling at Puget Sound for years, meaning the spill-risk reduction would phase in slowly rather than immediately.

Penalties are modest — civil fines capped at $25,000 per day and criminal exposure only for willful violations — which a skeptic could argue is too small to deter a large operator from cutting corners on spill readiness.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — a lower chance of a catastrophic spill in a productive marine environment, plus tested and publicly documented response plans — are large for the region and the costs, while real, are the ordinary price of operating oil vessels safely. The bill's most serious weakness is speed: because double hulls apply only to new tankers, protection builds gradually, and the modest penalty levels limit deterrence against the biggest operators.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 1989, and the committee never acted on it, so it expired when that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Brock Adams of Washington introduced the bill on April 19, 1989, citing concern over several recent Puget Sound oil spills and the inadequate response to the tanker accident in Prince William Sound, Alaska.

The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the same day — and no further action appears on the record for the rest of the 101st Congress.
The bill attracted a single cosponsor, a Senate Democrat, and never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or action in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil tanker owners and the oil-producing, refining, and transportation facilities around Puget Sound came out ahead: they avoided the double hull, contingency plan, inspection, and penalty requirements the bill would have imposed, because it never advanced beyond committee.

for.name: Sen. Brock Adams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put his state's marine safety concerns on the record

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in April 1989 and took no further recorded action on it for the remainder of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the record shows a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and no recorded opposition from any member or bloc.

industries.note: The bill would have required double hulls on new tankers, spill-prevention plans, mandated equipment, and annual inspections, with fines up to $25,000 per day for violations. Its death in committee spared them those costs, and the public got no added protection from this bill.

industries.industry: Petroleum refining and oil storage and transportation facilities
industries.note: Facilities that could reasonably be expected to spill into Puget Sound would have had to submit government-approved contingency plans sized to a published 'maximum probable spill' estimate. Because the bill died, they faced no new planning or approval requirement.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing and tourism in Puget Sound
industries.note: These industries depend on an unpolluted marine environment; the bill's spill prevention and response requirements were designed to protect the waters they work in. They gained nothing, however, because the bill never advanced.
